before.content_html:
What Is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism. The goal is to maintain optimum conditions for function — the best possible environment for enzyme action and all cell processes — despite constant changes happening both inside and outside the body.

The human body must keep several internal conditions within narrow limits. These include blood glucose concentration, body temperature, and water levels. If any of these drift too far from the optimum, enzymes cannot work efficiently, chemical reactions slow down or stop, and cells can be damaged or destroyed.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains optimal conditions for enzyme action and all cell functions. Without it, enzymes would denature and metabolic reactions would fail.

Control Systems

All homeostatic control systems — whether nervous or chemical — share three essential components. You must know these for the exam:

1. Receptors — cells that detect stimuli (changes in the environment). For example, temperature receptors in the skin detect when you touch something hot. 2. Coordination centres — such as the brain, spinal cord, and pancreas — that receive and process information from receptors. 3. Effectors — muscles or glands that bring about responses to restore optimum levels.

The body uses two types of automatic control system. Nervous responses are fast, short-lived, and travel as electrical impulses along neurones (e.g. pulling your hand away from a flame). Chemical (hormonal) responses are slower, longer-lasting, and travel in the blood (e.g. insulin controlling blood glucose). Both work through the same receptor → coordinator → effector pathway, but the speed and duration differ.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour. It detects changes in the environment using receptors, processes the information, and triggers appropriate responses.

Information from receptors passes along specialised cells called neurones as electrical impulses. These impulses travel to the central nervous system (CNS), which is made up of the brain and spinal cord. The CNS acts as the coordination centre — it processes the information and coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

Key Fact

The nervous pathway follows this sequence: \(stimulus \rightarrow receptor \rightarrow coordinator (CNS) \rightarrow effector \rightarrow response\). Learn this order — it appears in almost every exam question on this topic.

Types of Neurone

There are three types of neurone, each with a specific role in the nervous pathway:

Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. They have a long axon and a cell body branching off to one side. Relay neurones are found entirely within the CNS. They connect sensory neurones to motor neurones and allow the brain or spinal cord to process information. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors. They have a long axon and a cell body at one end with branching dendrites.

Synapses

Neurones do not physically touch each other. There is a tiny gap between them called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of one neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters. These chemicals diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This process converts an electrical signal into a chemical signal and back again.

Neurotransmitters are only released from one side of the synapse (the pre-synaptic neurone) and can only bind to receptors on the other side (the post-synaptic neurone). This means impulses can only travel in one direction, ensuring signals reach the correct destination. Some drugs and toxins work by mimicking or blocking neurotransmitters at synapses.

Reflex Actions

A reflex action is an automatic and rapid response to a stimulus. Reflex actions do not involve the conscious part of the brain — they are coordinated by the spinal cord. This makes them much faster than voluntary responses, which is essential for protecting the body from harm.

Examples include pulling your hand away from a hot plate, your pupil constricting in bright light, and blinking when an object moves towards your eye.

Key Fact

The reflex arc pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. Reflex actions bypass the conscious brain, making them automatic and fast enough to prevent injury.

1. The stimulus is heat from the hot plate. 2. Temperature receptors in the skin detect the heat. 3. An electrical impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord. 4. The impulse passes across a synapse to a relay neurone in the spinal cord. 5. The impulse passes across another synapse to a motor neurone. 6. The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector — a muscle in the arm. 7. The muscle contracts (response), pulling the hand away before the brain has even registered the pain.

Reaction Time

Reaction time is the time it takes for a person to respond to a stimulus. In humans, typical reaction times are between 0.2 and 0.9 seconds. Reaction time can be measured using a simple ruler-drop test — this is Required Practical 7 in the AQA specification.

Factors that can affect reaction time include age, gender, caffeine, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions. In the required practical, students investigate the effect of one factor (such as practice or distraction) on human reaction time using a ruler-drop method, then calculate the mean to improve reliability.

Method: One person holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark. A second person places their thumb and finger around the ruler at the 0 mark without touching it. The ruler is released without warning, and the catcher grabs it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls (in cm) is recorded. This is repeated at least 5 times and the mean distance is calculated.

Key points: The further the ruler falls, the slower the reaction time. To make it a fair test, the same ruler and same hand position should be used each time. Anomalous results (e.g. if the person anticipates the drop) should be identified and excluded before calculating the mean.
before.exam_tip_html: For AQA Trilogy questions on this topic, always use the correct sequence: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response. In “explain” questions about reflex arcs, name each type of neurone and describe what happens at each synapse. For “describe” questions about reaction time practicals, remember to mention calculating the mean and identifying anomalous results — examiners expect these terms.

before.content_html:
Hormones in Human Reproduction

The human endocrine system controls reproduction through a group of hormones produced by the pituitary gland and the ovaries. Understanding how these hormones interact is essential for this topic — the exam often asks you to describe the roles of individual hormones and explain how they control the menstrual cycle.

During puberty, the pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain) begins releasing hormones that trigger the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In males, the testes produce testosterone, which stimulates sperm production and causes changes such as a deeper voice, facial hair, and increased muscle mass. In females, the ovaries begin producing oestrogen, which triggers egg maturation and changes such as breast development, widening of the hips, and the start of the menstrual cycle.

Key Fact

Four hormones control the menstrual cycle: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone), LH (luteinising hormone), oestrogen, and progesterone. FSH and LH are produced by the pituitary gland. Oestrogen and progesterone are produced by the ovaries.

The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle lasts approximately 28 days and is controlled by the interaction of the four key hormones. It prepares the body for pregnancy each month. If no fertilisation occurs, the cycle resets.

Days 1–4 — Menstruation: The uterus lining breaks down and is shed through the vagina as a period. Hormone levels are low at this stage.

Days 4–14 — Repair and build-up: FSH is released by the pituitary gland and causes an egg to mature inside a follicle in the ovary. The maturing follicle produces oestrogen, which causes the uterus lining to thicken with blood vessels, ready to receive a fertilised egg.

Day 14 — Ovulation: A surge in LH triggers ovulation — the release of the mature egg from the ovary into the fallopian tube. High oestrogen levels stimulate the pituitary gland to release this surge of LH.

Days 14–28 — Maintenance: After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels fall, and the lining is shed — the cycle starts again.

Hormone Interactions — Negative Feedback

The four hormones do not work in isolation — they interact through negative feedback. This means rising levels of one hormone can inhibit (reduce) the production of another, keeping the cycle in balance.

FSH stimulates oestrogen production. Rising oestrogen then inhibits further FSH release (so only one egg usually matures). At the same time, high oestrogen stimulates LH release, which triggers ovulation. After ovulation, progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH — preventing another egg from being released while the body waits to see if pregnancy occurs. When progesterone drops (because the corpus luteum breaks down), FSH is no longer inhibited and the cycle restarts.

Key Fact

Oestrogen inhibits FSH but stimulates LH. Progesterone inhibits both FSH and LH. This negative feedback loop ensures only one egg matures per cycle and prevents multiple ovulations.

Contraception

Contraception means preventing pregnancy. The specification requires you to know about hormonal and non-hormonal methods, and to be able to evaluate their effectiveness, side effects, and suitability.

Oral contraceptive pill: Contains hormones (oestrogen and/or progesterone). The combined pill contains both hormones — it prevents ovulation by maintaining high oestrogen and progesterone, which inhibits FSH and LH release. The progesterone-only pill thickens cervical mucus to prevent sperm reaching the egg. Effectiveness: over 99% if used correctly. Possible side effects include headaches, nausea, and blood clots (rare).

Contraceptive injection: A slow-release injection of progesterone given every 8–13 weeks. It inhibits ovulation and thickens cervical mucus. Very effective but cannot be reversed quickly once injected. May cause irregular periods.

Contraceptive implant: A small flexible rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm. It releases progesterone slowly for up to 3 years. Over 99% effective. May cause irregular bleeding in some users.

Contraceptive patch: A skin patch that releases oestrogen and progesterone through the skin. Changed weekly for three weeks, then a week off. Effectiveness: 99.8%. Side effects similar to the combined pill.

Condoms (male and female): Barrier methods that physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms are 98% effective when used correctly and are the only method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). No hormonal side effects.

Diaphragm or cap: A flexible dome placed over the cervix before sex. Used with spermicide. Around 92–96% effective. Must be fitted correctly and left in place for several hours after sex.

Intrauterine device (IUD): A small T-shaped device inserted into the uterus by a doctor. The copper IUD releases copper ions that are toxic to sperm and also prevents a fertilised egg from implanting. Over 99% effective and lasts 5–10 years. It is non-hormonal but can cause heavier periods.

Surgical methods: Sterilisation involves cutting or tying the fallopian tubes (female) or the vas deferens (male vasectomy). Permanent and highly effective. Difficult to reverse.

Abstinence and natural family planning: Avoiding sex during the fertile window (around ovulation). No side effects but requires careful monitoring of the cycle and is less reliable than other methods.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraception works by maintaining high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, which inhibit FSH and LH through negative feedback — preventing ovulation. Barrier methods physically block sperm from reaching the egg. Only condoms protect against STIs.

The Use of Hormones to Treat Infertility (Higher Tier)

Infertility affects many couples. Hormones can be used to help women who have difficulty conceiving. Two main treatments involve reproductive hormones:

FSH and LH injections (fertility drugs): Women who do not ovulate naturally can be given FSH to stimulate egg maturation, followed by LH to trigger ovulation. This is called fertility treatment. A risk is that multiple eggs may be released, increasing the chance of multiple births (twins, triplets), which carry higher health risks for both mother and babies.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation): IVF is a more involved process. The woman is given FSH and LH to stimulate the ovaries to produce several eggs. These eggs are then collected surgically and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory dish. The fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and one or two are transferred into the woman’s uterus. Remaining embryos can be frozen for future use.

Benefits: IVF allows couples who cannot conceive naturally to have children. Success rates have improved over time. Embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before implantation. Unused embryos can be stored for later attempts.

Drawbacks: IVF is emotionally and physically demanding for the woman. Success rates are not guaranteed — typically around 30% per cycle for women under 35, lower for older women. The hormone treatment can cause side effects such as hot flushes, headaches, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Multiple embryos may implant, leading to multiple births. There are ethical concerns about the fate of unused embryos — some people believe life begins at fertilisation and object to embryos being destroyed or frozen indefinitely. IVF is also expensive, with NHS funding varying by area.

knowledge_checks.q: Which hormone causes an egg to mature inside a follicle in the ovary?
Which is the only method of contraception that also protects against sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces _____.
In IVF, eggs are fertilised with sperm in a _____ dish, not inside the body.
Match each hormone to its role in the menstrual cycle:
right: Causes egg to mature in the ovary
Maintains the uterus lining after ovulation

before.exam_tip_html: AQA commonly asks you to compare contraceptive methods or evaluate IVF. For “compare and explain” questions, always state the similarity or difference clearly, then explain why using your knowledge of hormones. For extended response questions on IVF, structure your answer with benefits on one side and drawbacks on the other, and finish with a conclusion. Remember that IVF content is Higher Tier only — if you are sitting Higher, expect a question on it.

before.content_html:
Two Types of Reproduction

All living organisms reproduce to pass on their genes to the next generation. There are two fundamentally different ways this can happen: sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction. Understanding the differences between them is essential for AQA Biology Paper 2.

Sexual reproduction involves the fusion (joining together) of two special sex cells called gametes. In animals, the male gamete is the sperm cell and the female gamete is the egg cell (ovum). In plants, pollen contains the male gamete and the ovule contains the female gamete. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, they form a single cell called a zygote, which then divides to form an embryo. Because each parent contributes different genetic information, the offspring show genetic variation — they are genetically unique.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction produces offspring that are genetically different from each other and from both parents. This genetic variation is important because it helps populations adapt to changing environments through natural selection.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent. There is no fusion of gametes. The offspring are produced by mitosis and are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Many organisms use asexual reproduction: bacteria divide by binary fission, plants can reproduce by runners or bulbs, and some animals such as starfish can regenerate from fragments.

Sexual reproduction: Two parents needed. Gametes fuse at fertilisation. Offspring are genetically varied. Involves meiosis. Slower process. Advantages — variation helps species survive environmental changes and resist disease.

Asexual reproduction: One parent only. No gamete fusion. Offspring are clones (genetically identical). Involves mitosis. Faster process. Advantages — only one parent needed, rapid population growth when conditions are favourable.

Some organisms, such as fungi, malarial parasites, and many plants, can switch between both types depending on conditions. When conditions are good, asexual reproduction is faster. When conditions change, sexual reproduction introduces variation that may help some offspring survive.

Meiosis — Making Gametes

Meiosis is the special type of cell division that produces gametes. It takes place in the reproductive organs — the ovaries and testes in animals, and the flower in plants. Meiosis is different from mitosis in several important ways.

Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs. These are called diploid cells. Before meiosis begins, the DNA replicates so that each chromosome is copied. The cell then divides twice: the first division separates the pairs of chromosomes, and the second division separates the copies. The result is four daughter cells, each with half the normal chromosome number — 23 chromosomes in humans. These cells are called haploid.

Key Fact

Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells that are all genetically different. Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells that are genetically identical. The AQA exam frequently asks you to compare these two types of cell division.

Meiosis introduces genetic variation in two ways. First, when chromosome pairs line up before the first division, they do so randomly — each gamete gets a different combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Second, sections of DNA can be swapped between paired chromosomes in a process called crossing over. These two mechanisms mean that every gamete produced by meiosis is genetically unique.

When a sperm cell (23 chromosomes) fuses with an egg cell (23 chromosomes) at fertilisation, the full diploid number is restored — the zygote has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). This is why gametes must be haploid: if they were diploid, the chromosome number would double with every generation.

DNA — The Molecule of Life

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made of two strands twisted into a double helix shape. Each strand is made of repeating units called nucleotides. A nucleotide consists of a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).

The two strands of DNA are held together by complementary base pairing: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. This is why DNA can replicate accurately — each strand acts as a template for making a new complementary strand. The order of bases along a strand forms the genetic code that carries the instructions for building proteins.

DNA molecules are very long. In human cells, the DNA is tightly coiled and packed into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs — one chromosome in each pair comes from the mother and one from the father.

A gene is a short section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which are assembled into a specific protein. Different genes code for different proteins, and it is these proteins that determine our characteristics — from eye colour to blood type to enzyme function.

Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. For example, the gene for eye colour has alleles for brown, blue, and green. Because chromosomes come in pairs, you inherit two alleles for every gene — one from each parent. Whether you display the characteristic depends on which alleles you have and whether they are dominant or recessive.

The Human Genome

The genome is the entire set of genetic material in an organism. The Human Genome Project was a major international research effort completed in 2003 that mapped the entire sequence of human DNA. Scientists identified approximately 20,000–25,000 genes across 3 billion base pairs of DNA.

Understanding the human genome has enormous benefits for science and medicine. It allows scientists to search for genes linked to specific diseases, develop personalised medicines that target an individual’s genetic makeup, trace human migration patterns across history, and identify how closely related different species are through evolutionary biology.

Key Fact

The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) identified all the genes in human DNA. Key benefits include: identifying genes linked to disease, developing targeted medicines, understanding evolutionary relationships, and advancing forensic science.

Medicine: Doctors can identify people who carry genes for inherited disorders (such as cystic fibrosis or Huntington’s disease) before symptoms appear. This enables genetic screening and counselling, and may lead to gene therapy treatments.

Pharmacogenomics: Medicines can be tailored to an individual’s genetic profile, making treatments more effective with fewer side effects. This is sometimes called personalised or precision medicine.

Evolution and ancestry: Comparing genomes of different species shows how closely related they are. More similar genomes indicate a more recent common ancestor. Scientists have also traced human migration out of Africa by studying patterns in modern genomes.

Forensics: DNA profiling uses specific sections of an individual’s genome to create a unique “genetic fingerprint,” used in criminal investigations and paternity testing.

flashcard_questions.q: A short section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein and therefore a specific characteristic.
Thread-like structures made of DNA found in the nucleus of a cell. Humans have 23 pairs (46 total).
Different versions of the same gene. For example, the gene for eye colour has alleles for brown and blue.
_____ 1 in 4 (25%) chance of BB (homozygous dominant — brown eyes)

flashcard_questions.a: The combination of alleles an organism has for a particular gene, written using letters such as Bb or ff.

before.exam_tip_html: In AQA Trilogy exams, you will often be given a Punnett square to complete or interpret. Always label your alleles clearly (capital for dominant, lowercase for recessive), show all four offspring genotypes, and state the probability as a ratio, fraction, or percentage. For “explain” questions about inherited disorders, make sure you state whether the allele is dominant or recessive, give the genotypes of affected individuals and carriers, and use a Punnett square if the question asks you to predict outcomes.

before.content_html:
Levels of Organisation in an Ecosystem

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (the biotic components) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. To understand how ecosystems work, you need to know the hierarchy of organisation.

An individual organism is a single living thing. A population is all the organisms of one species in an area. A community is all the populations of different species in an area. An ecosystem includes both the community and the abiotic factors such as temperature, light, water, soil, and pH.

Key Fact

Remember the hierarchy: \(organism \rightarrow population \rightarrow community \rightarrow ecosystem\). Exam questions often ask you to define each level or explain the difference between a community and an ecosystem (a community is just the living organisms; an ecosystem also includes the abiotic environment).

Within an ecosystem, organisms compete for resources. Animals compete for food, territory, water, and mates. Plants compete for light, water, space, and mineral ions from the soil. Species that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — this is natural selection at work within the ecosystem.

Abiotic factors (non-living) include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH, wind speed, carbon dioxide concentration, and oxygen levels in water. Changes in abiotic factors can affect the distribution and abundance of organisms — for example, plants grow faster in higher light intensities.

Biotic factors (living) include food availability, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and competition from other species. For example, the introduction of grey squirrels to the UK led to a decline in red squirrels because greys outcompete them for food and carry squirrel pox.

How Materials Are Cycled

Materials in an ecosystem are constantly recycled. Living organisms take in materials, use them, and return them to the environment when they die and decompose. Two key cycles you need to know are the carbon cycle and the water cycle.

The carbon cycle: Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis in plants and algae. Carbon is passed along food chains when animals eat plants and other animals. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere through respiration (by all living organisms), combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and decomposition of dead organisms by microorganisms. Some carbon becomes locked in fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) or sedimentary rocks (limestone) for millions of years.

The water cycle: Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and rivers, and transpires from plants. Water vapour rises, cools, and condenses to form clouds. Precipitation (rain, snow) falls back to the surface, where it flows into rivers or soaks into groundwater, eventually returning to the sea. This cycle is powered by energy from the sun.

Key Fact

Decomposition is essential to both cycles. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead plant and animal material, releasing carbon dioxide through respiration and returning mineral ions to the soil. Without decomposition, nutrients would be locked in dead organisms and unavailable for new growth.

What Is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity is the variety of all living species in an ecosystem or on Earth as a whole. High biodiversity means a wide range of different species are present. Ecosystems with high biodiversity are more stable and more resilient to environmental change because if one species is lost, others can fill its role in the food web.

Scientists measure biodiversity by studying the number of different species in an area (species richness) and the abundance of each species. To estimate population size in a habitat, scientists use sampling techniques such as quadrats placed randomly and transects to study distribution. Random sampling avoids bias and makes results more representative.

Quadrats: A 0.5m × 0.5m frame placed on the ground at random positions (using random number generators to pick coordinates). Count the number of organisms of each species inside the quadrat. Repeat in multiple positions and calculate a mean. To estimate total population: mean count per quadrat × total area ÷ area of one quadrat.

Transects: A measuring tape is laid in a straight line across a habitat (e.g. from a pond edge up a hillside). Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the line to record how species distribution changes with distance. This is useful for investigating the effect of an abiotic factor that changes across the habitat (e.g. light, moisture).

Human Threats to Biodiversity

The human population is growing rapidly, and our activities are reducing biodiversity worldwide. The spec identifies several key threats.

Waste management: Humans produce large quantities of waste. Unless properly handled, this pollutes water (sewage, fertiliser runoff causing eutrophication), air (smoke, acidic gases), and land (landfill, toxic chemicals). Pollution kills organisms directly and destroys habitats.

Land use: Building, quarrying, farming, and dumping waste all reduce the amount of land available for other organisms. As the human population grows, more land is converted for agriculture, housing, and industry, destroying natural habitats and reducing biodiversity.

Key Fact

Deforestation in tropical areas has severe consequences: loss of habitat for millions of species, release of stored carbon (increasing atmospheric CO₂), loss of trees that would absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis, and disruption of the water cycle (less transpiration means less rainfall). Large-scale deforestation in the Amazon and Southeast Asia is a major driver of both biodiversity loss and climate change.

Global warming: The burning of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, and farming livestock produces methane — both are greenhouse gases that trap heat in the Earth’s atmosphere. This leads to rising global temperatures, which cause sea level rise (from melting ice caps and thermal expansion), changes in the distribution of species, loss of polar habitats, more extreme weather events, and changes in migration patterns and breeding seasons.

Short-wave radiation from the sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The Earth re-emits this energy as long-wave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb some of this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth. This keeps the planet warm enough to support life — the natural greenhouse effect. However, human activities have increased the concentration of greenhouse gases, enhancing the greenhouse effect and causing average global temperatures to rise.

Maintaining Biodiversity

Scientists and governments recognise that biodiversity must be actively protected. The specification requires you to know programmes and strategies for maintaining biodiversity at local, national, and global levels.

Breeding programmes: Zoos and wildlife centres run captive breeding programmes for endangered species, then reintroduce them to the wild. Examples include the red kite in the UK and the Arabian oryx. Seed banks: Organisations like the Millennium Seed Bank store seeds from thousands of plant species to protect genetic diversity and allow future reintroduction if species become extinct in the wild.

Protected areas: National parks, nature reserves, and marine conservation zones protect habitats from development and allow ecosystems to recover. Hedgerow and habitat restoration: Farmers are encouraged (sometimes through government grants) to maintain hedgerows, field margins, and wildlife corridors that connect fragmented habitats.

Legislation: Laws such as the Wildlife and Countryside Act (1981) make it illegal to harm protected species or damage their habitats. Recycling and waste reduction: Reducing the amount of waste going to landfill limits habitat destruction and pollution. Sustainable development: Meeting the needs of the current population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This includes sustainable forestry (replanting trees), sustainable fishing (quotas to prevent overfishing), and reducing carbon emissions through renewable energy.

Global agreements: International cooperation is essential because biodiversity loss and climate change are global problems. Agreements such as the Paris Agreement (2015) aim to limit global temperature rise. The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) restricts the trade of threatened animals and plants across borders.

Key Fact

The conflict between human needs and biodiversity is a common 6-mark question topic. You should be able to discuss how measures like breeding programmes, seed banks, protected areas, and legislation help maintain biodiversity — and acknowledge that these measures can conflict with economic development (e.g. farmers losing land to nature reserves, or industries restricted by environmental regulations).

lessons.title: The Brain, the Eye and Temperature Control

before.content_html:
The Human Brain

The brain is the most complex organ in the human body. It is made up of billions of interconnected neurones and is responsible for controlling everything from conscious thought to automatic body functions like breathing and heart rate.

Scientists have mapped the brain into distinct regions, each with specialised roles. Understanding what each part does helps doctors diagnose and treat neurological conditions. However, the brain is incredibly difficult to study because of its complexity — and because any investigation carries a risk of causing damage.

Key Fact

The brain controls complex behaviour and has different regions that carry out different functions. Scientists have been able to map these regions to particular functions by studying patients with brain damage, by electrically stimulating different parts of the brain, and by using MRI scanning techniques.

Regions of the Brain

The brain has three main regions you need to know for your exam:

The cerebral cortex is the large, folded outer layer of the brain. It is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language. When you think, plan, remember facts or speak, it is your cerebral cortex at work. The folds increase its surface area, giving more space for neurones to carry out complex processing.

The cerebellum sits at the back and underneath the cerebral cortex. It is responsible for the coordination of muscular activity, balance and posture. It does not initiate movement but ensures your muscles work together smoothly — for example, when you walk or catch a ball.

The medulla oblongata (often called simply the medulla) is found at the base of the brain, where it connects to the spinal cord. It controls unconscious activities that keep you alive, such as breathing rate, heart rate and the movement of food through the digestive system (peristalsis). These activities happen automatically without you thinking about them.

Studying the brain is challenging. Scientists cannot simply open up a living brain to observe it, and damage to brain tissue can have severe consequences. Techniques such as MRI scanning allow researchers to observe which parts of the brain are active during different tasks without causing harm.

Key Fact

The treatment and investigation of brain disorders is difficult because the brain is so complex and delicate. Any damage to brain tissue can have significant and unpredictable consequences.

The Structure of the Eye

The eye is a sense organ containing receptors that are sensitive to light. Light enters the eye and is focused onto the back of the eye, creating an image that the brain interprets.

The key structures of the eye and their functions are:

  • Cornea — the transparent front layer that refracts (bends) light as it enters the eye. The cornea does most of the eye’s focusing.
  • Iris — the coloured part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil. The iris contains muscles that contract or relax to adjust how much light enters.
  • Pupil — the hole in the centre of the iris through which light passes. In bright light, the iris contracts and the pupil gets smaller. In dim light, the iris relaxes and the pupil gets larger.
  • Lens — a transparent, flexible structure behind the iris. The lens fine-focuses light onto the retina by changing shape.
  • Retina — the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing receptor cells. The retina converts the focused light into electrical impulses.
  • Optic nerve — carries electrical impulses from the retina to the brain, where the image is processed.

Accommodation — Focusing on Near and Distant Objects

accommodation is the process by which the eye changes the shape of the lens to focus on objects at different distances. Two structures work together to make this happen: the ciliary muscles and the suspensory ligaments.

When you look at something far away, the ciliary muscles relax. This allows the suspensory ligaments to become taut (pulled tight). The taut ligaments pull on the lens, making it thin. A thin lens refracts light less, which is correct for distant objects where the light rays entering the eye are nearly parallel.

When you look at something close up, the ciliary muscles contract. This releases tension on the suspensory ligaments, which become slack (loose). The lens springs back into a fat, rounded shape. A thicker lens refracts light more, bending the diverging light rays from a near object so they focus on the retina.

Key Fact

To focus on a near object: ciliary muscles contract → suspensory ligaments go slack → lens becomes fat and round. To focus on a distant object: ciliary muscles relax → suspensory ligaments pull taut → lens becomes thin and flat. Many students get this the wrong way around in exams.

Thermoregulation — Controlling Body Temperature

The human body must maintain a core temperature of approximately 37°C. This is the optimum temperature for enzymes to work effectively. If body temperature rises too high or falls too low, enzymes can denature and vital chemical reactions will slow down or stop — which can be fatal.

The thermoregulatory centre in the brain (specifically the hypothalamus) monitors the temperature of the blood flowing through it. It also receives nerve impulses from temperature receptors in the skin. When body temperature deviates from 37°C, the thermoregulatory centre triggers responses to bring it back to normal.

When body temperature rises above 37°C, several mechanisms act to cool the body down:

  • vasodilation — blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen (dilate). This allows more blood to flow close to the skin surface, increasing the transfer of thermal energy to the environment by radiation.
  • Sweating — sweat glands release sweat onto the skin surface. As the water in sweat evaporates, it absorbs thermal energy from the skin, cooling the body down.
  • Hairs lie flat — erector muscles relax so body hairs lie flat against the skin. This reduces the layer of insulating air trapped next to the body, allowing more heat to escape.

When body temperature drops below 37°C, the body responds in the opposite way:

  • vasoconstriction — blood vessels near the skin surface narrow (constrict). Less blood flows near the surface, so less thermal energy is lost to the surroundings by radiation.
  • Shivering — muscles contract and relax rapidly and involuntarily. The metabolic reactions involved in muscle contraction require energy from respiration, which releases thermal energy as a by-product, warming the body.
  • Hairs stand up — erector muscles contract, pulling body hairs upright. This traps a thicker layer of insulating air close to the skin, reducing heat loss. This is sometimes called piloerection and causes “goosebumps.”
Key Fact

Thermoregulation is an example of a negative feedback mechanism. The thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus detects a change from the set point (37°C) and triggers responses that counteract the change, returning body temperature to normal. This is essential because enzymes denature at high temperatures and work too slowly at low temperatures.

lessons.title: The Kidney, Water Balance and Plant Hormones

before.content_html:
The Kidney and Its Role in Excretion

The body produces waste products that must be removed to prevent toxic build-up. This removal process is called excretion. The two main metabolic waste products are carbon dioxide (removed by the lungs) and urea, which is produced in the liver when excess amino acids are broken down in a process called deamination. Urea is then dissolved in the blood and carried to the kidneys for removal.

The kidneys perform two critical jobs: they filter waste products out of the blood, and they regulate the water and ion content of the body. Each kidney contains around one million tiny filtering units called nephrons.

Key Fact

The three main functions of the kidney are: filtration of the blood to remove waste, selective reabsorption of useful substances back into the blood, and excretion of urea, excess water, and ions as urine.

How the Nephron Works

Blood enters the kidney through the renal artery and flows into a tiny knot of capillaries called the glomerulus, which sits inside a cup-shaped structure called the Bowman’s capsule. The blood arriving at the glomerulus is under high pressure because the blood vessel leaving the glomerulus (the efferent arteriole) is narrower than the one entering it (the afferent arteriole). This high pressure forces small molecules — water, glucose, urea, and ions — out of the blood and into the Bowman’s capsule. Large molecules such as proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through and stay in the blood. This stage is called ultrafiltration.

After filtration, the liquid (called filtrate) passes along the kidney tubules. Here, useful substances are reabsorbed back into the blood by selective reabsorption. All glucose is reabsorbed by active transport. The correct amount of water is reabsorbed — the amount depends on the body’s needs and is controlled by the hormone ADH. Some ions (such as sodium) are selectively reabsorbed. Urea is not reabsorbed — it stays in the tubule and is excreted as part of urine.

If glucose appears in urine, it can be a sign of diabetes. In diabetes, blood glucose levels are too high for the kidneys to reabsorb all the glucose, so some passes into the urine.

Water Balance and ADH

The water content of the blood must be carefully controlled. If cells gain or lose too much water by osmosis, they cannot function properly — they may swell and burst, or shrink and become damaged. The regulation of water balance is part of osmoregulation.

Water balance is controlled by a negative feedback loop involving the hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone). When the blood becomes too concentrated (for example, after sweating or not drinking enough), receptors in the hypothalamus detect this change. The hypothalamus signals the pituitary gland to release more ADH into the blood. ADH travels to the kidneys and causes the tubules to become more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood. The result is a small volume of concentrated urine.

When the blood is too dilute (for example, after drinking a lot of water), less ADH is released. The kidney tubules stay less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed. The result is a large volume of dilute urine. This is a classic example of negative feedback — the system automatically corrects itself to maintain a stable internal environment.

Key Fact

More ADH = more water reabsorbed = small volume of concentrated urine. Less ADH = less water reabsorbed = large volume of dilute urine. The hypothalamus monitors blood concentration; the pituitary gland releases ADH.

Kidney Failure: Dialysis and Transplants

If both kidneys fail, waste products such as urea build up in the blood and water balance is lost. Without treatment, kidney failure is fatal. There are two options: kidney dialysis or a kidney transplant.

In dialysis, the patient’s blood is passed through a machine containing a partially permeable membrane. On the other side of the membrane flows dialysis fluid, which has the same concentration of glucose and useful ions as normal blood, but contains no urea. Urea and excess ions diffuse from the blood (high concentration) across the membrane into the dialysis fluid (low concentration) down a concentration gradient. The dialysis fluid flows in the opposite direction to the blood to maintain a steep concentration gradient along the whole length of the membrane. Glucose is not removed because its concentration in the dialysis fluid matches the blood.

Advantages: Dialysis keeps patients alive while waiting for a transplant and is widely available. Disadvantages: Treatment takes 3–4 hours, three times per week. Patients must follow a restricted diet. There is a risk of infection at the point where blood leaves and re-enters the body. It is expensive for the NHS in the long term.

A kidney transplant replaces a failed kidney with a healthy one from a donor. The donor can be a living relative or someone who has recently died (deceased donor). The donor kidney must be a close tissue match to reduce the risk of rejection, where the recipient’s immune system attacks the new kidney as if it were a foreign pathogen.

Advantages: A successful transplant frees the patient from dialysis and dietary restrictions, allowing a much more normal life. It is cheaper for the NHS in the long term. Disadvantages: There is a shortage of donor kidneys and long waiting lists. The patient must take immunosuppressant drugs for life to prevent rejection, which increases the risk of infections. There are also risks from the surgery itself.

Plant Hormones: Auxins and Tropisms

Plants cannot move to find better conditions, but they can grow towards or away from stimuli such as light and gravity. These directional growth responses are called tropisms. Tropisms are controlled by plant hormones, particularly auxin.

Phototropism is the growth response to light. Shoots show positive phototropism — they grow towards the light. Auxin is produced in the tip of the shoot. When light hits one side, auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot. This higher concentration of auxin on the shaded side causes cells there to elongate more, bending the shoot towards the light source.

Key Fact

In shoots, auxin promotes cell elongation (more auxin = more growth). In roots, auxin inhibits cell elongation (more auxin = less growth). This opposite effect explains why shoots grow towards light but roots grow downwards.

Gravitropism (also called geotropism) is the growth response to gravity. Roots show positive gravitropism — they grow downwards, towards gravity. When a root grows horizontally, auxin accumulates on the lower side. Because auxin inhibits cell elongation in roots, the lower side grows more slowly than the upper side, causing the root to bend downwards. Shoots show negative gravitropism — they grow upwards, away from gravity.

Gibberellins are plant hormones involved in seed germination, stem elongation, and flowering. They stimulate the breakdown of starch stores in seeds, providing energy for the embryo to begin growing. Gibberellins can also promote the growth of seedless fruit.

Ethene is a gaseous hormone that promotes fruit ripening. It is used commercially to ripen bananas and tomatoes after they have been transported while still unripe. Plants also use auxins in weedkillers: synthetic auxins cause broad-leaved weeds to grow uncontrollably and die, while narrow-leaved grasses are less affected.

Cress seeds are grown on damp cotton wool in Petri dishes. Dish A is placed in a box with light entering from one side only. Dish B receives even light from above (control). Dish C is kept in the dark. After 3–5 days, the shoots in Dish A bend towards the light source (positive phototropism), Dish B grows straight upwards, and Dish C shows random or reduced growth. The independent variable is the direction of light; the dependent variable is the direction and length of shoot growth.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels and Transfer of Biomass

before.content_html:
What Are Trophic Levels?

All organisms in an ecosystem can be placed into trophic levels depending on how they get their food. The word “trophic” comes from the Greek word for feeding. Understanding trophic levels helps us see how energy and biomass move through an ecosystem.

Trophic level 1 — Producers: Producers are organisms that make their own food using energy from the Sun through photosynthesis. All green plants and algae are producers. They form the base of every food chain because they convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.

Trophic level 2 — Primary consumers: Primary consumers are herbivores that eat producers. Examples include rabbits, caterpillars, and zooplankton. They obtain energy by digesting the biomass of the plants they eat.

Trophic level 3 — Secondary consumers: Secondary consumers are carnivores or omnivores that eat primary consumers. Examples include frogs, small birds, and foxes.

Trophic level 4 — Tertiary consumers: Tertiary consumers are top predators that eat secondary consumers. Examples include hawks, sharks, and lions. They sit at the top of the food chain and are rarely eaten by other animals.

Key Fact

Trophic levels always follow the same order: producers → primary consumers → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers. Each level depends on the one below it for energy.

Food Chains and Food Webs

A food chain is a simple diagram that shows the transfer of energy from one organism to the next in a single pathway. The arrows in a food chain always point in the direction that energy flows — from the organism being eaten to the organism doing the eating. For example: grass → rabbit → fox → eagle.

In reality, most organisms eat more than one type of food and are eaten by more than one predator. A food web shows these interconnected feeding relationships. Food webs give a more realistic picture of an ecosystem because they show how changes in one population can affect many other species.

Food chains are useful for showing a single pathway of energy transfer, but they oversimplify feeding relationships. For instance, a rabbit does not only eat grass — it also eats clover, dandelions, and other plants. Similarly, a fox does not only eat rabbits — it also eats voles, birds, and berries.

Food webs show these multiple connections. If a disease kills the rabbit population, a food web helps predict that foxes might switch to eating more voles, and the plants rabbits used to eat would increase in number. Exam questions often ask you to predict the effect of removing one species from a food web.

Pyramids of Biomass

A pyramid of biomass represents the total biomass at each trophic level in a food chain. Each bar is drawn to scale, with the producer level at the bottom and the top predator at the top. The width of each bar represents the amount of biomass at that level.

Pyramids of biomass almost always form a pyramid shape — wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. This is because biomass is lost at every trophic level, so there is always less biomass at higher levels than at lower ones.

Key Fact

Pyramids of biomass are more reliable than pyramids of numbers. A single oak tree (one organism) can support thousands of caterpillars, which would make a pyramid of numbers look inverted — but the pyramid of biomass still shows the tree has more biomass than all the caterpillars combined.

How Is Biomass Lost Between Trophic Levels?

Not all the biomass from one trophic level is transferred to the next. In fact, a large proportion is lost at each stage. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — by the time energy has passed through several levels, there is not enough biomass left to support another level of consumers.

Biomass and energy are lost between trophic levels in several ways:

Not all organisms are eaten: Some organisms die of old age, disease, or other causes before being consumed by the next trophic level. Their biomass passes to decomposers instead.

Not all parts are digested: Some materials, such as bones, teeth, hair, feathers, and cellulose from plant cell walls, cannot be digested. These are egested as faeces and become available to decomposers rather than being absorbed by the consumer.

Energy is used in life processes: Organisms at every trophic level use energy from the biomass they consume for respiration. This energy is used for movement, maintaining body temperature (especially in mammals and birds), growth, reproduction, and other metabolic processes. The energy released by respiration is transferred to the surroundings as heat and cannot be passed to the next trophic level.

Excretory products: Organisms produce waste products such as urea (in urine) and carbon dioxide. These contain energy and biomass that are lost from the food chain.

As a rough guide, only about 10% of the biomass (and the energy it contains) at one trophic level is passed on to the next. This is sometimes called the 10% rule. For example, if producers contain 10,000 kJ of energy, primary consumers receive approximately 1,000 kJ, secondary consumers receive approximately 100 kJ, and tertiary consumers receive only about 10 kJ.

This explains why top predators are always rare — there simply is not enough energy reaching the top of the food chain to support large populations. It also explains why food chains rarely exceed four or five trophic levels.

Calculating Efficiency of Biomass Transfer

The specification requires you to calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer between trophic levels. The formula is:

\(Efficiency = (\text{biomass transferred to the next level} \div \text{biomass at the previous level}) \times 100\)

For example, if producers contain 5,000 kg of biomass and primary consumers contain 600 kg, the efficiency of transfer is: (600 ÷ 5,000) × 100 = 12%.

Key Fact

Learn the efficiency formula: (biomass at next level ÷ biomass at previous level) × 100. You may also be asked to rearrange it to calculate how much biomass is transferred or how much was available at the previous level.

A grassland ecosystem contains the following biomass at each trophic level: grass = 8,000 kg, grasshoppers = 720 kg, frogs = 85 kg, snakes = 9 kg.

\(Grass \rightarrow grasshoppers:\) (720 ÷ 8,000) × 100 = 9.0%

\(Grasshoppers \rightarrow frogs:\) (85 ÷ 720) × 100 = 11.8%

\(Frogs \rightarrow snakes:\) (9 ÷ 85) × 100 = 10.6%

Notice how all the values are roughly around 10%, which supports the 10% rule as an approximation.

Why Does This Matter for Food Security?

Understanding biomass transfer has practical implications for feeding the human population. Because energy is lost at every trophic level, eating plants (trophic level 1) is a more efficient way to feed people than eating animals (trophic level 2 or higher). For example, the same area of farmland used to grow grain could feed far more people directly than if the grain were first fed to cattle and the cattle then eaten.

This is one reason why some scientists argue that reducing meat consumption could help address global food security challenges. However, grazing animals can use land that is not suitable for growing crops, and animal products are important sources of essential nutrients.

Decomposition and Decay

All living organisms eventually die. When they do, their bodies — along with waste products such as faeces and urine — are broken down by organisms called decomposers. The two main types of decomposer are bacteria and fungi. Both are microorganisms — they are too small to see without a microscope.

Larger organisms called detritus feeders (detritivores) also play a role. Maggots, earthworms, woodlice, and beetles eat dead organic matter and produce waste. Bacteria and fungi then break down everything — the dead organism, the detritivores, and their waste — releasing carbon dioxide, water, and mineral ions back into the environment.

Decomposers work by secreting enzymes onto the dead organic material. These enzymes break down large molecules (such as carbohydrates and proteins) into smaller, soluble molecules that the decomposers can absorb and use as food. This process of decomposition is essential because it recycles elements like carbon and nitrogen so they can be reused by living organisms.

Key Fact

Without decomposers, dead organisms and waste would pile up, and essential elements such as carbon and nitrogen would become locked away and unavailable to plants. The decay cycle ensures these nutrients are constantly recycled.

Factors Affecting the Rate of Decomposition

Decomposition does not always happen at the same speed. Three main factors affect how quickly organic matter is broken down:

Temperature: Decomposers use enzymes, and enzymes work fastest at an optimum temperature (around 37°C for many bacteria). Below this, particles move slowly and there are fewer successful collisions between enzyme and substrate. Above the optimum, the enzyme is denatured — its active site changes shape permanently, so the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.

Moisture: Water is needed for enzymes to be secreted and for the products of digestion to be absorbed. Dry conditions slow decomposition dramatically — this is why dried foods like ship’s biscuits lasted for months on long sea voyages.

Oxygen availability: Most decomposers respire aerobically, so they need oxygen. More oxygen means faster decomposition. However, some microorganisms can respire anaerobically (without oxygen), producing methane and carbon dioxide — this is the basis of biogas production.

In this practical, you use lipase to model decomposition. Milk is mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator (which turns pink in alkaline conditions). Lipase is added at different temperatures. As the lipase breaks down the fats in milk into fatty acids, the pH drops and the indicator loses its pink colour. You time how long this takes at each temperature.

Key variables: Independent variable = temperature. Dependent variable = time for the indicator to turn colourless (or rate of decay = 1 ÷ time). Control variables = volume of milk, volume of lipase, volume of indicator. Expected result: Rate increases up to the optimum temperature, then drops sharply as the enzyme is denatured.

Compost and Biogas

Gardeners and farmers make use of decomposition in two practical ways. Compost is made from dead plant material (grass cuttings, leaves, vegetable peelings) that is broken down by decomposers in aerobic conditions. The resulting material is rich in mineral ions such as nitrates, which act as a natural fertiliser and improve soil quality for growing crops.

Biogas is produced when organic waste (manure, sewage, crop waste) is decomposed anaerobically inside a sealed container called a biogas generator. The main product is methane, which is flammable and can be used for heating, cooking, or generating electricity. Biogas is a renewable fuel because the organic waste can be continually replaced.

Food Security

Food security means having enough food to feed a population. The global demand for food is rising, and several biological and environmental factors threaten our ability to meet it.

Key Fact

Threats to food security include: increasing birth rate, changing diets in developed countries (more meat consumption), new pests and pathogens affecting crops and livestock, environmental changes (climate change, drought, flooding), conflict and poverty, and the cost of agricultural inputs such as fertilisers and machinery.

To address these threats, scientists and farmers are developing sustainable ways to produce more food without depleting natural resources.

Making Food Production More Efficient

At each stage of a food chain, biomass is lost through respiration (releasing energy for movement and body heat), excretion, and undigested material in faeces. Shorter food chains are more efficient because less energy is wasted between trophic levels. Eating less meat and more plant-based food reduces the number of stages in the food chain, making food production more efficient overall.

Farmers can increase the growth rate of food animals by restricting their movement (so less energy is lost in movement), keeping them indoors in warm conditions (so less energy is used maintaining body temperature), and providing high-protein feed. These intensive methods are efficient but raise ethical objections: animals have less space, cannot exhibit natural behaviours, and overcrowding can lead to the spread of disease and increased antibiotic use.

Since 2024, UK legislation has banned the routine use of antibiotics on farm animals to help prevent antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics may only be used in exceptional circumstances for disease prevention.

Sustainable Fisheries

Sustainable food production means producing food in ways that meet current needs without harming the ability to produce food in the future. For fishing, this means managing fish stocks so they do not collapse.

Strategies include: setting fishing quotas to limit how many fish can be caught, controlling net mesh sizes so young fish can escape and breed, banning fishing during breeding seasons, and using fish farming (aquaculture) to rear fish in controlled environments. Fish farms manage feeding, water quality, and disease to maximise growth efficiently.

Overfishing removes fish faster than populations can reproduce. Modern fishing technology (sonar, GPS, large trawl nets) has made it easier to locate and catch huge quantities. Rising global populations and changing diets have increased demand. Without careful management, fish populations can collapse entirely, destroying both ecosystems and the livelihoods of fishing communities.

Biotechnology: Mycoprotein

Biotechnology offers solutions to food security. One key example is mycoprotein, a protein-rich food produced from the fungus Fusarium venenatum. It is grown in large fermenters under aerobic conditions, using glucose syrup as a food source. The fungal biomass is harvested, purified, and processed into products sold under the brand name Quorn™.

Mycoprotein is high in protein and fibre, low in saturated fat, and has a texture similar to chicken. It provides a sustainable alternative to meat because it can be produced quickly in controlled conditions, using far less land and water than animal farming. However, some people may be allergic to it, and it must be clearly labelled.

Key Fact

Mycoprotein production: Fusarium venenatum fungus → grown in fermenters with glucose syrup + oxygen → harvested, purified, and processed into Quorn™. It is high in protein and fibre, low in fat, and suitable for vegetarians.

Biotechnology: GM Crops

GM crops (genetically modified crops) are plants whose DNA has been changed using genetic engineering. A gene for a desirable characteristic is cut from one organism using a restriction enzyme, inserted into a plasmid (a small ring of bacterial DNA that acts as a vector), and transferred into the plant cells.

Examples of GM crop traits include: resistance to insect pests (reducing the need for chemical pesticides), resistance to herbicides (allowing farmers to spray weeds without harming the crop), improved nutritional content (such as Golden Rice, which contains beta-carotene to combat vitamin A deficiency), and increased crop yield.

Advantages: Higher crop yields can help feed growing populations. Pest-resistant crops reduce pesticide use, benefiting the environment. Crops can be engineered to grow in harsh conditions (drought, poor soil). Improved nutritional content can address malnutrition in developing countries.

Disadvantages: GM genes could transfer to wild plant populations through cross-pollination, creating “superweeds.” Long-term effects on human health are not fully understood. Biodiversity may be reduced if GM crops replace traditional varieties. Farmers may become dependent on seed companies, as GM seeds are often patented and cannot be saved for replanting.
